_note: Curated example projects: small builds — home-network and security gadgets plus beginner robotics. Shown in the gallery (CLI --gallery, web 'Gallery' tab) and used by the offline mock provider. Same shape as what the LLM returns, plus id + tags (+ optional tutorial link).

projects.title: Pi-hole Ad Blocker
projects.summary: A tiny Raspberry Pi that blocks ads and trackers for every device on your home Wi-Fi (phones, laptops, smart TVs) by acting as your network's DNS server.

steps.title: Flash the SD card
steps.detail: In Raspberry Pi Imager choose Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). In the settings set a hostname (pihole), your Wi-Fi, a username and password, and enable SSH. Write the card.

steps.title: Boot and connect
steps.detail: Put the card in the Pi, power it, wait two minutes, then from your computer run: ssh <username>@pihole.local

steps.title: Give it a fixed address
steps.detail: In your router's admin page, find the Pi in the list of connected devices and add a DHCP reservation, so its IP address never changes.

steps.title: Install Pi-hole
steps.detail: Update first (sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y), then run the official installer: curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash. Accept the defaults and note the admin address it shows at the end.

steps.title: Set the admin password
steps.detail: Run sudo pihole setpassword, then open http://pihole.local/admin in a browser and log in to the dashboard.

steps.title: Point your network at it
steps.detail: In the router's DHCP/DNS settings, set the Pi's IP address as the only DNS server. Reconnect your devices to Wi-Fi so they pick up the change.

steps.title: Test and tune
steps.detail: Open a news site: ads should be gone and the dashboard's 'Queries blocked' counter should rise. If a site breaks, find its domain in Query Log and click Allow.

safetyNotes: If the Pi is off, websites stop loading for everyone. Plug it into a reliable socket, or keep a note of how to switch the router's DNS back.
Don't add a public DNS server as a second DNS in the router: devices would use it to go around Pi-hole.

projects.title: Ultrasonic Radar Sweep
projects.summary: A servo sweeps the ultrasonic sensor back and forth and your laptop draws a live radar screen of nearby objects.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: controls the sweep and takes readings

steps.title: Mount the sensor
steps.detail: Glue or tape the HC-SR04 onto the servo horn so it rotates with it.

steps.title: Wire it up
steps.detail: Servo signal→D9, servo power→5V/GND (one SG90 is fine on USB power). HC-SR04 TRIG→D10, ECHO→D11.

steps.title: Sweep and measure
steps.detail: Loop the servo from 15° to 165° and back in 2° steps; at each step wait 30 ms, then measure distance.

steps.title: Stream the data
steps.detail: Print 'angle,distance' lines over Serial at 115200 baud.

steps.title: Draw the radar
steps.detail: Run the Python viewer (pyserial + matplotlib polar plot) that reads the lines and draws fading green dots.

steps.title: Calibrate
steps.detail: Place an object at a measured 30 cm and check the plot; adjust the speed-of-sound constant if it's off.

projects.title: Obstacle-Avoiding Robot Car
projects.summary: A two-wheeled robot that drives around on its own: when its ultrasonic 'eyes' see a wall, it stops, looks left and right, and turns toward the side with more space.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: the brain: drives and decides where to turn

parts.name: 2WD robot car chassis kit
parts.purpose: frame, 2 TT gear motors, wheels and caster

parts.name: L298N / TB6612 motor driver
parts.purpose: powers both motors forward and backward

parts.name: SG90 micro servo
parts.purpose: turns the sensor to look left and right

parts.name: 18650 Li-ion cell
parts.purpose: about 7.4 V for motors and Arduino

steps.title: Build the chassis
steps.detail: Assemble the kit: motors, wheels and caster on the base plate. Fix the Arduino, motor driver and battery holder on top with screws or double-sided tape.

steps.title: Wire the motors
steps.detail: L298N: left motor to OUT1/OUT2, right motor to OUT3/OUT4. ENA→D5, IN1→D7, IN2→D8, ENB→D6, IN3→D4, IN4→D2.

steps.title: Wire the power
steps.detail: Battery + to the L298N 12V input, battery − to its GND. With the 5V jumper on, the L298N's 5V pin powers the Arduino: connect it to the Arduino 5V, and GND to GND.

steps.title: Mount the eyes
steps.detail: Glue the HC-SR04 onto the servo horn at the front. Servo signal→D3, red→5V, brown→GND. HC-SR04 TRIG→A0, ECHO→A1 (analog pins work as digital pins).

steps.title: Drive and avoid
steps.detail: Drive forward and measure every 50 ms. Closer than 25 cm: stop, reverse for 0.3 s, turn the servo to 150° and 30° to measure both sides, then turn toward the side with more space for about 0.4 s.

steps.title: Tune it
steps.detail: Motors are never identical: if the car drifts, lower the faster side's PWM value (e.g. 170 vs 180) until it drives straight.

safetyNotes: 18650 cells are powerful: use a holder with no bare contacts, never short them, and charge them with a proper charger.
Test on the floor, not on a table it can drive off.

projects.title: DIY Security Key
projects.summary: Turn a Raspberry Pi Pico into a FIDO2 USB security key you can use for passkeys and two-factor login, with open-source firmware.

parts.name: USB cable
parts.purpose: connects it to your computer (data cable, not charge-only)

parts.name: Small case or heat-shrink tube
parts.purpose: protects the board on your keyring

steps.title: Download the firmware
steps.detail: From the pico-fido project's Releases page on GitHub, download the .uf2 file built for your board (Raspberry Pi Pico / RP2040).

steps.title: Flash it
steps.detail: Hold the white BOOTSEL button while plugging the Pico in. It appears as a USB drive called RPI-RP2; drag the .uf2 file onto it. The board restarts as a security key.

steps.title: Set a PIN
steps.detail: In Chrome go to Settings → Privacy and security → Security → Manage security keys → Create a PIN (Windows: Settings → Accounts → Sign-in options → Security key).

steps.title: Try it safely
steps.detail: Open webauthn.io, register, then log in. When the browser asks you to touch the key, press the BOOTSEL button, which pico-fido uses as the 'touch' confirmation.

steps.title: Use it on a real account
steps.detail: Add it as an extra security key on an account that supports passkeys or FIDO2 (Google, GitHub, Microsoft). Keep your existing 2FA method as a backup.

steps.title: Make it pocket-proof
steps.detail: Slide the board into a small case or heat-shrink tube and put it on your keyring.

safetyNotes: This is a learning project: the Pico has no secure chip, so someone with the key in hand could read its secrets. Always keep a backup login method.

projects.title: Mini Robot Arm
projects.summary: A 4-servo desk robot arm you control with four knobs, and it can record your moves and replay them on its own at the press of a button.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: reads the knobs and moves the servos

parts.name: 4-DOF acrylic robot arm kit
parts.purpose: the arm frame: base, shoulder, elbow, gripper

parts.name: SG90 micro servo
parts.purpose: one per joint (MG90S metal-gear servos are sturdier)

steps.title: Center the servos first
steps.detail: Before building, upload a sketch that sets all four servos to 90°. Then assemble the arm kit with every joint in its middle position, so each servo can move both ways.

steps.title: Wire the knobs
steps.detail: Each potentiometer: outer legs to 5V and GND, middle leg to A0, A1, A2 and A3 (base, shoulder, elbow, gripper).

steps.title: Wire the servos
steps.detail: Signals to D3, D5, D6 and D9. Servo red and brown wires go to the 5 V / 2 A supply on the breadboard rails, and the supply GND connects to Arduino GND.

steps.title: Find safe limits
steps.detail: For each joint, slowly turn its knob and note the angles where it would hit the frame. Map the knob (0–1023) only to that safe range, so a servo never pushes against the frame.

steps.title: Smooth movement
steps.detail: Average the last few knob readings and move each servo at most 2° per step, every 15 ms, so the arm glides instead of jerking.

steps.title: Record and replay
steps.detail: A short button press saves the current 4 angles (up to 100 poses). A long press plays them back in a loop; press again to stop.

safetyNotes: A servo pushing against the frame draws a lot of current and gets hot. Set the angle limits before long sessions.
Don't power four servos from the Arduino's 5V pin; use the separate supply.

projects.title: RFID Access Lock
projects.summary: Tap the right card and a servo opens the latch on your drawer or box; tap the wrong one and it beeps red. After 5 wrong tries it locks out for 30 seconds.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: checks the card and drives the latch

parts.name: RC522 RFID reader + tags
parts.purpose: reads the card or key fob

steps.title: Wire the reader
steps.detail: RC522 runs on 3.3 V: 3.3V→3.3V (not 5V!), GND→GND, RST→D9, SDA(SS)→D10, MOSI→D11, MISO→D12, SCK→D13.

steps.title: Wire latch, LEDs and buzzer
steps.detail: Servo signal→D6, red→5V, brown→GND. Green LED→D7, red LED→D8 through 220 Ω resistors. Buzzer + →D5, − →GND.

steps.title: Read your card IDs
steps.detail: Install the MFRC522 library, upload the sketch and open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. Tap each card; it prints its UID.

steps.title: Allow your cards
steps.detail: Copy the UIDs of the cards you want to accept into the ALLOWED list at the top of the sketch and upload again.

steps.title: Build the latch
steps.detail: Glue the servo inside the box lid so its horn swings behind a small block on the box wall. Find the 'open' and 'closed' angles and set them in the sketch.

steps.title: Test the lockout
steps.detail: Tap an unknown card 5 times: the red LED should blink and every card is ignored for 30 seconds.

safetyNotes: A card's UID alone is easy to copy with a cheap cloner, so this is a learning lock for a drawer, not for a door.
Keep a way to open the box without the reader (a hidden screw), in case the battery or code fails.

projects.title: Bluetooth RC Car
projects.summary: Drive a little robot car from your phone: a free Bluetooth controller app sends forward, back, left and right to the Arduino.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: turns phone commands into motor moves

parts.name: 2WD robot car chassis kit
parts.purpose: frame, 2 TT gear motors, wheels and caster

parts.name: Resistor
parts.purpose: 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ voltage divider for the HC-05 RX pin

steps.title: Build the car
steps.detail: Assemble the chassis kit and wire the L298N exactly as in the Obstacle-Avoiding Car: ENA→D5, IN1→D7, IN2→D8, ENB→D6, IN3→D4, IN4→D2, battery to the L298N, its 5V to the Arduino.

steps.title: Wire the Bluetooth module
steps.detail: HC-05 VCC→5V, GND→GND, TXD→D10. Its RXD is 3.3 V only: connect Arduino D11 → 1 kΩ → HC-05 RXD, and RXD → 2 kΩ → GND.

steps.title: Read commands
steps.detail: Use SoftwareSerial on D10/D11 at 9600 baud. Read one character at a time: F, B, L, R = drive, S = stop, digits 0–9 = speed.

steps.title: Pair your phone
steps.detail: Android: pair with 'HC-05' in Bluetooth settings (PIN 1234 or 0000), then connect from a free 'Arduino Bluetooth RC car' controller app.

steps.title: Fail safe
steps.detail: If no command arrives for 500 ms, stop the motors, so the car doesn't drive away when the phone disconnects.

safetyNotes: iPhones can't connect to the classic HC-05. For iPhone, use a BLE module such as the HM-10 and a BLE controller app instead.
Handle 18650 cells with care and charge them with a proper charger.

projects.title: Home VPN with WireGuard
projects.summary: Your own VPN server at home: on public Wi-Fi your phone sends everything through an encrypted tunnel to your house, and gets your Pi-hole ad blocking on the go.

parts.name: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W
parts.purpose: VPN server (a Raspberry Pi 4 with Ethernet is faster)

steps.title: Prepare the Pi
steps.detail: Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite with SSH enabled (as in the Pi-hole build) and give the Pi a DHCP reservation in your router. You can run the VPN on the same Pi as Pi-hole.

steps.title: Install WireGuard
steps.detail: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y wireguard qrencode. Then create keys for the server and your phone: wg genkey | tee server.key | wg pubkey > server.pub (repeat with phone.key / phone.pub).

steps.title: Write the server config
steps.detail: Create /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf with Address = 10.8.0.1/24, ListenPort = 51820, the server private key, and a [Peer] for the phone (its public key, AllowedIPs = 10.8.0.2/32). Add PostUp/PostDown iptables MASQUERADE rules so the phone can reach the internet through the Pi.

steps.title: Turn on forwarding and start
steps.detail: Set net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 in /etc/sysctl.conf (apply with sudo sysctl -p), then sudo systemctl enable --now wg-quick@wg0.

steps.title: Open one port
steps.detail: In the router, forward UDP port 51820 to the Pi's IP. If your home IP changes, set up a free dynamic-DNS name (for example DuckDNS) for it.

steps.title: Connect your phone
steps.detail: Write phone.conf (Address = 10.8.0.2/32, DNS = the Pi's IP, the server's public key, Endpoint = your-home-address:51820, AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0), show it as a QR code with qrencode -t ansiutf8 < phone.conf and scan it in the WireGuard app.

steps.title: Test from outside
steps.detail: Switch the phone to mobile data, turn the tunnel on and open a website. The WireGuard app shows data flowing; sudo wg on the Pi shows the phone's latest handshake.

safetyNotes: Forward only UDP 51820, nothing else, and keep the Pi updated (sudo apt full-upgrade).
Treat phone.conf like a password: delete it from the Pi after scanning, and remove a lost phone's [Peer] block straight away.

projects.title: Desk Crab — a 4-servo walking robot
projects.summary: A palm-sized quadruped that shuffles across your desk and backs away from obstacles it 'sees' with the ultrasonic sensor.

parts.name: Arduino Uno
parts.purpose: brain: gait timing and obstacle logic

parts.name: Battery holder (4×AA or 2×18650)
parts.purpose: separate 6 V supply for the servos

steps.title: Build the frame
steps.detail: Glue two popsicle sticks into a cross for the body. Hot-glue one servo at each arm end, horns facing outward.

steps.title: Attach the legs
steps.detail: Screw a servo horn onto each servo and glue a popsicle-stick leg to it, angled ~30° down so the body sits 3 cm off the desk.

steps.title: Wire the servos
steps.detail: Signal wires to D3, D5, D6, D9. Servo + and − go to the AA pack via the breadboard rails — NOT to the Arduino 5 V pin. Connect the pack's − to Arduino GND (common ground).

steps.title: Wire the sensor
steps.detail: HC-SR04: VCC→5V, GND→GND, TRIG→D10, ECHO→D11. Mount it on the front of the body with a dab of glue.

steps.title: Center and calibrate
steps.detail: Upload a sketch that writes 90° to every servo, then re-seat the horns so all legs point straight. Note any per-leg offset in an array.

steps.title: Write the gait
steps.detail: Use a 4-phase creep gait: lift-swing one leg at a time in order FL, BR, FR, BL. Store poses in a table and step through them every 150 ms with millis() instead of delay().

steps.title: Add obstacle avoidance
steps.detail: Read distance every 100 ms; if < 15 cm, play the gait table backwards for 2 s, then turn by running only the left legs.

steps.title: Test and tune
steps.detail: Run on a non-slip surface. If it drags, increase the lift angle; if it tips, shorten the swing range.

safetyNotes: Power the servos from the battery pack: four servos stalling at once can brown out or damage the Arduino's regulator.
Hot glue is hot enough to burn — let joints cool before handling.

projects.title: Door Tamper Alarm
projects.summary: A magnetic sensor on your door or drawer: when it's opened while armed, the ESP32 beeps and sends a notification to your phone.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: watches the sensor, sends the alert over Wi-Fi

steps.title: Wire the sensor
steps.detail: Reed switch between GPIO27 and GND, with INPUT_PULLUP. Door closed (magnet near) = LOW, door open = HIGH.

steps.title: Wire buzzer, LED and button
steps.detail: Buzzer on GPIO25, LED through 220 Ω on GPIO26, button from GPIO4 to GND (INPUT_PULLUP).

steps.title: Arm and disarm
steps.detail: The button toggles 'armed'. Give yourself 20 seconds to leave after arming, and 15 seconds after the door opens to disarm before the alarm goes off.

steps.title: Phone notifications
steps.detail: Install the free ntfy app and subscribe to a long random topic name. On alarm, the ESP32 sends an HTTP POST to https://ntfy.sh/<your-topic> with the message 'Door opened!'.

steps.title: Mount it
steps.detail: Stick the reed switch on the frame and the magnet on the door, less than 1 cm apart when closed. Test that opening the door triggers it.

safetyNotes: Anyone who knows an ntfy topic name can read it, so use a long random name and don't put personal details in messages.

projects.title: Laser Tripwire Alarm
projects.summary: A laser beam across a doorway hits a light sensor on the other side. When someone walks through and breaks the beam, a buzzer sounds until you reset it.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: Laser module S→D7 (so the Arduino can switch it), − →GND. LDR from 5V to A0, 10 kΩ from A0 to GND. Buzzer→D8, button from D2 to GND (INPUT_PULLUP).

steps.title: Shield the sensor
steps.detail: Put the LDR at the end of a short dark tube (a straw or rolled paper) so room light hardly reaches it and only the laser dot does.

steps.title: Aim
steps.detail: Place the laser on one side of the doorway at ankle height and the sensor on the other. Adjust until the dot sits right on the LDR.

steps.title: Calibrate
steps.detail: Print analogRead(A0) with the beam on and off. Set the alarm threshold halfway between the two values.

steps.title: Arm and alarm
steps.detail: Pressing the button arms the alarm after 5 seconds. If the reading drops below the threshold for more than 50 ms, sound the buzzer until the button is pressed again.

safetyNotes: Never look into the laser or point it at people's or pets' eyes. Mount it low (ankle height) and use only a low-power module.

projects.title: Hardware Password Generator
projects.summary: Press a button, get a strong random password or passphrase on a small screen, made by the ESP32's hardware random-number generator. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: OLED on I2C (SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22, VCC→3V3, GND→GND). Buttons from GPIO4 and GPIO5 to GND, INPUT_PULLUP.

steps.title: Use real randomness
steps.detail: Call esp_random() for random numbers. It is a true hardware RNG while Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is on; with radios off, call bootloader_random_enable() first.

steps.title: Pick characters fairly
steps.detail: For each character, draw a random number and reject it if it falls above the largest multiple of your alphabet size (rejection sampling), so no character is more likely than another.

steps.title: Passphrase mode
steps.detail: The second button switches to 5 random words from a word list (for example the EFF short word list stored in flash): easier to type, still strong.

steps.title: Show the strength
steps.detail: Display the length and the entropy in bits (length × log2(alphabet size)). Aim for at least 80 bits.

safetyNotes: Type the password straight into your password manager and press the button again so it disappears from the screen.

projects.title: Smart Trash Can
projects.summary: Wave your hand near the bin and the lid opens by itself; it closes gently a few seconds after you're done. No more touching a dirty lid.

parts.name: Arduino Nano
parts.purpose: watches for a hand and moves the lid

parts.name: HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor
parts.purpose: detects your hand in front of the bin

parts.name: SG90 micro servo
parts.purpose: lifts a light lid (use an MG996R for a heavy one)

parts.name: Small trash bin with hinged lid

steps.title: Mount the sensor
steps.detail: Fix the HC-SR04 on the front of the bin, facing outward, about two thirds of the way up. TRIG→D9, ECHO→D10, VCC→5V, GND→GND.

steps.title: Mount the servo
steps.detail: Glue the servo next to the lid hinge so its horn pushes the lid up from below. Signal→D6; power it from the battery pack with a shared GND.

steps.title: Find the angles
steps.detail: Upload a test sketch and find the 'closed' angle (horn flat) and 'open' angle (lid up, ~100°).

steps.title: Open on a wave
steps.detail: Measure every 100 ms. Closer than 15 cm: open the lid. Keep it open until no hand has been seen for 3 seconds.

steps.title: Close gently
steps.detail: Close in 2° steps every 15 ms instead of all at once, so the lid doesn't slam.

safetyNotes: Keep the electronics and battery pack above the bin, away from liquids.

projects.title: Automatic Pet Feeder
projects.summary: A food container with a servo flap that drops a portion at set times every day, plus a button for an extra snack (limited to a few per day).

parts.name: DS3231 real-time clock module
parts.purpose: knows the time, even after a power cut

steps.title: Build the hopper
steps.detail: Cut the bottom off a large plastic bottle and mount it upside down as a funnel. Glue a cardboard or plastic flap to the servo horn so it covers the bottle's neck.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: DS3231: SDA→A4, SCL→A5, VCC→5V, GND→GND. Servo signal→D9, power from the 5 V supply (shared GND). Button from D2 to GND (INPUT_PULLUP).

steps.title: Set the clock once
steps.detail: With the RTClib library, set the DS3231 to your computer's time once. Its coin battery keeps the time afterwards.

steps.title: Feeding schedule
steps.detail: Store feeding times in an array (for example 7:30 and 18:00). At each time, open the flap for about 0.6 s, then close it.

steps.title: Calibrate the portion
steps.detail: Weigh what falls out in one opening and adjust the open time until it matches your pet's portion.

steps.title: Snack button
steps.detail: The button gives a small portion, at most 3 times a day and not more often than every 30 minutes.

safetyNotes: Watch the first few days in person, and don't rely on it alone while you're away for long.
Make sure your pet can't get a paw or tongue near the moving flap.

projects.title: Laser Cat Toy
projects.summary: A tiny pan-tilt turret that moves a laser dot around the floor in random paths for five minutes, so your cat can hunt it.

parts.name: Pan-tilt servo bracket
parts.purpose: holds two servos for left/right and up/down

steps.title: Build the turret
steps.detail: Assemble the pan-tilt bracket with both servos centered at 90°. Glue the laser module on the top plate, pointing forward.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: Pan servo→D9, tilt servo→D10, laser S→D7, button from D2 to GND. Servos and laser share 5V/GND.

steps.title: Mount it
steps.detail: Put it on a shelf about 1 m up, pointing down at the floor in front of it.

steps.title: Keep the dot on the floor
steps.detail: Find the tilt angles where the dot is between 0.5 m and 2 m away on the floor, and never allow tilt outside that range.

steps.title: Random paths
steps.detail: Pick a random target inside the allowed area, glide there 1° at a time, pause 0.2–1.5 s, repeat. Mix fast dashes and slow creeps.

steps.title: Play sessions
steps.detail: The button starts a 5-minute session; then the laser turns off. End sessions with a real toy for the cat to 'catch'.

safetyNotes: Never let the beam reach eye level: limit the tilt so the dot always stays on the floor, and only use a low-power module.
Only run it while you're in the room.

projects.title: Mini Biped Walker
projects.summary: A small two-legged robot with hips and ankles that waddles forward, dances and turns away from walls — a first step towards a bigger walking robot.

steps.title: Build the body
steps.detail: Make a box for the head/body that holds the Nano, battery pack and sensor. Hip servos mount under the box, vertical shafts; each ankle servo hangs off its hip horn, horizontal shaft, with a flat foot glued to its horn.

steps.title: Wire everything
steps.detail: Servos: left hip D2, right hip D3, left ankle D4, right ankle D5; power from the battery pack, shared GND. HC-SR04 TRIG→D8, ECHO→D9. Buzzer→D10.

steps.title: Find home positions
steps.detail: Center all servos at 90°, re-seat horns so the robot stands straight with feet flat. Store the per-servo trim offsets in an array.

steps.title: Walk with sine waves
steps.detail: Drive each joint as angle = home + A·sin(2πt/T + φ). Ankles: A ≈ 25°, in phase (rocks the weight side to side). Hips: A ≈ 30°, shifted by +90° phase. T ≈ 1 s per step.

steps.title: Tune balance
steps.detail: If it falls sideways, reduce ankle amplitude; if it shuffles in place, increase the hip amplitude or the phase shift.

steps.title: Add behaviours
steps.detail: Walk forward; when the wall is < 20 cm, chirp, step back 3 times and turn (asymmetric hip amplitude). Add a 'dance' that plays with the phases.

safetyNotes: Disconnect the servo battery while uploading code so the robot doesn't jump off the table.

projects.title: Air Theremin
projects.summary: Play notes by moving your hand above an ultrasonic sensor; a potentiometer picks the musical scale.

steps.title: Wire the sensor
steps.detail: HC-SR04: VCC→5V, GND→GND, TRIG→D9, ECHO→D10.

steps.title: Wire the buzzer and pot
steps.detail: Buzzer + to D8, − to GND. Potentiometer outer legs to 5V and GND, wiper to A0.

steps.title: Measure distance
steps.detail: Send a 10 µs TRIG pulse, read ECHO with pulseIn(), convert to cm (duration / 58). Clamp to 5–50 cm.

steps.title: Map distance to notes
steps.detail: Split 5–50 cm into 8 zones and map each to a note of the selected scale (major, minor, pentatonic — chosen by the pot reading).

steps.title: Play
steps.detail: Call tone(8, frequency) when the note changes; noTone(8) when no hand is detected for 300 ms.

steps.title: Smooth it
steps.detail: Average the last 5 readings so the pitch doesn't jitter between notes.

projects.title: Desk Weather Station
projects.summary: A tiny OLED dashboard showing temperature, humidity and pressure with a 'rain coming?' trend arrow based on the pressure change over 3 hours.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: reads the sensor, drives the display

steps.title: Share the I2C bus
steps.detail: Both modules: VCC→3V3, GND→GND, SDA→GPIO21, SCL→GPIO22. They have different addresses (BME280 0x76, OLED 0x3C), so they can share the two wires.

steps.title: Scan the bus
steps.detail: Upload an I2C scanner sketch and check both addresses appear in the Serial Monitor before writing any other code.

steps.title: Read the sensor
steps.detail: Use the Adafruit BME280 library; read every 5 s. Note: a sensor mounted right next to the ESP32 reads 1–2 °C warm — keep them a few cm apart.

steps.title: Draw the dashboard
steps.detail: With Adafruit SSD1306: big temperature on top, humidity and pressure below, and an arrow (↑ / → / ↓) for the pressure trend.

steps.title: Pressure trend
steps.detail: Store one pressure sample every 10 minutes in an 18-slot ring buffer (3 hours). A drop of more than 3 hPa over 3 hours means weather is likely getting worse.

projects.title: Plant Watering Buddy
projects.summary: An ESP32 watches the soil moisture of one plant, waters it with a tiny pump when it gets dry and shows the moisture history on a web page on your Wi-Fi.

parts.name: ESP32 dev board
parts.purpose: reads the sensor, runs the pump and a small web server

parts.name: Capacitive soil moisture sensor
parts.purpose: measures how wet the soil is (no corrosion, unlike resistive probes)

parts.name: Mini 5 V water pump + tubing
parts.purpose: moves water from a jar to the pot

parts.name: 5 V / 2 A power supply
parts.purpose: powers the pump (and the ESP32 via USB)

steps.title: Wire the sensor
steps.detail: Sensor VCC→3V3, GND→GND, AOUT→GPIO34 (an ADC1 pin — ADC2 pins don't work while Wi-Fi is on).

steps.title: Calibrate dry and wet
steps.detail: Print analogRead(34) with the probe in air (dry value, ~3000) and in a glass of water (wet value, ~1200). Map readings to 0–100 % between those two numbers.

steps.title: Wire relay and pump
steps.detail: Relay VCC→5V (VIN), GND→GND, IN→GPIO26. Pump + goes through the relay's COM/NO contacts to the 5 V supply; pump − to supply GND. Share GND with the ESP32.

steps.title: Watering logic
steps.detail: Every 10 minutes: if moisture < 30 %, run the pump for 3 s, then wait at least 30 minutes before watering again so the water has time to soak in. Never run the pump more than 5 times per day (safety cap).

steps.title: Web dashboard
steps.detail: Connect to Wi-Fi and serve a page with the current moisture and the last 24 readings (keep them in a ring buffer) using the WebServer library.

steps.title: Test without the plant
steps.detail: Put the probe in a cup, let it dry, check the pump triggers once and stops. Only then place it in the real pot, with the pump tube clipped to the pot's edge.

safetyNotes: Keep the electronics above and away from the water; put the board in a box or bag.
Mini pumps burn out if they run dry — keep the reservoir filled or add a water-level check.

projects.title: ESP32-CAM Video Doorbell
projects.summary: A doorbell button with a tiny camera: when someone presses it, you get a phone notification with a photo of who's at the door.

parts.name: ESP32-CAM-MB USB programmer
parts.purpose: uploads code to the ESP32-CAM over USB

parts.name: Small weatherproof box
parts.purpose: case with a hole for the lens

steps.title: Program it
steps.detail: Plug the ESP32-CAM onto the MB programmer, select the 'AI Thinker ESP32-CAM' board in the Arduino IDE and upload the CameraWebServer example to check the camera works.

steps.title: Wire the button
steps.detail: Button between GPIO13 and GND (INPUT_PULLUP). GPIO13 is free on the AI Thinker board when the SD card isn't used.

steps.title: Take a photo
steps.detail: On a button press (debounced), grab a frame with esp_camera_fb_get() at VGA size.

steps.title: Send it to your phone
steps.detail: Install the ntfy app and subscribe to a long random topic. Send the JPEG with an HTTP PUT to https://ntfy.sh/<your-topic> with the header 'Filename: door.jpg'. It arrives as a notification with the picture.

steps.title: Box it
steps.detail: Mount it in the box with the lens behind a small hole and the button on the front. A 5 V USB charger nearby powers it.

safetyNotes: Point the camera only at your own doorstep, and check your local rules about recording shared hallways or the street.
Anyone who knows the ntfy topic name can see the photos: use a long random name, or your own ntfy server.
